analogy.p: Imagine every metal as a person who, when startled by a loud noise (the heat of the flame), always gives out a particular coloured flash. Sodium always flashes yellow, copper always flashes green. By seeing which colour is flashed, you can tell who is in the room. The analogy breaks down because in a mixture several people might flash at once and the loudest (sodium) can drown out the others, and because the flash is really electrons dropping energy levels, not a decision by the metal.

bullets: **Lithium, Li+** → **crimson (deep red)** flame.
**Sodium, Na+** → **yellow** flame.
**Potassium, K+** → **lilac (pale purple)** flame.
**Calcium, Ca2+** → **orange-red** flame.
**Copper(II), Cu2+** → **green** flame.
Flame tests identify the **metal ion (cation)** in a compound, not the non-metal part.
The test is **qualitative**: it tells you which ion is present, not how much.
Know the method, the five colours, and the limitations; these are the typical mark-scoring points.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know (triple science only)
core.p: AQA 4.8.3 (Identification of ions by chemical and spectroscopic means; **separate science only**) states that **flame tests can be used to identify metal ions**. You must know the colours given by five ions: **lithium (crimson), sodium (yellow), potassium (lilac), calcium (orange-red) and copper(II) (green)**. You must also know how a flame test is carried out, and that if a sample contains a **mixture of ions** some flame colours can be **masked**, which is a limitation. Flame tests link to the wider idea that elements can be identified by instrumental methods (flame emission spectroscopy).

bullets: **Heat energy** from the flame excites electrons in the metal ion.
The electrons **return to lower energy levels** and **emit light** (extension, not required for the mark).
Different metals have different electron arrangements and so emit **different colours**.
The colour is characteristic of the **metal**, so any compound of that metal (chloride, nitrate, carbonate) gives the same flame colour.
The colour is produced by the **ion**, which is why a flame test identifies the **positive ion** only.
The same principle explains the colours in **fireworks**: metal compounds are chosen for the colours they give.
Flame emission spectroscopy (see 'Instrumental methods') uses exactly this idea but analyses the light with a spectrometer.
Link to the periodic table: lithium, sodium and potassium are **Group 1** metals; calcium is **Group 2**; copper is a **transition metal**.
core.h: Why different metal ions give different flame colours
core.p: When a metal compound is heated in a hot Bunsen flame, the energy of the flame **excites electrons** in the metal ions into higher energy levels. These electrons then fall back to lower energy levels and **release the extra energy as light**. Each metal has its own set of energy levels, so each emits light of particular wavelengths, and our eyes see a characteristic colour. This is why the flame colour acts like a fingerprint for the metal. You do not need the electron explanation for GCSE, but it helps you understand why the test works and why instrumental methods (which split the light into a spectrum) are more reliable.

bullets: **Step 1: Clean the wire loop** by dipping it in **dilute hydrochloric acid** and holding it in the Bunsen flame; repeat until the flame shows **no colour**.
**Step 2: Dip the clean loop** into the sample (a solid compound or a solution of the metal compound), so a little sticks to the wire.
**Step 3: Hold the loop in the hot blue part of the Bunsen flame** (a clear, non-luminous flame).
**Step 4: Observe the colour** of the flame and record it.
**Step 5: Clean the wire again** (acid then flame) before testing another sample, to avoid contamination.
Alternative to a wire: a **wooden splint** soaked in water or a sample, passed through the flame (the splint must not burn too much).
Use a **blue (non-luminous) flame** because a yellow flame would hide the colours.
Always keep the hydrochloric acid and the test solutions separate, to avoid cross-contamination.
core.h: The flame test method, step by step
core.p: A flame test must be done carefully so the colour you see comes only from the sample you are testing. The standard method uses a **nichrome (or platinum) wire loop**, cleaned in acid, a Bunsen burner with a **roaring blue flame**, and a small amount of the sample. Learn the steps in order because a method question usually awards a mark for cleaning the wire and a mark for observing the colour.

bullets: **Li+ → crimson** (a deep, rich red). Mnemonic: **L**ithium is **L**ovely red.
**Na+ → yellow** (bright, persistent yellow-orange). Sodium is very common so this colour is very strong.
**K+ → lilac** (a pale pinkish-purple, a faint colour easily masked).
**Ca2+ → orange-red** (a brick-red or orange-red colour).
**Cu2+ → green** (sometimes described as blue-green).
The ions are given as **cations**: Li+, Na+, K+, Ca2+, Cu2+.
Know the charge on each: Group 1 ions are 1+, calcium is 2+, copper(II) is 2+.
Do not confuse **crimson (lithium)** with **orange-red (calcium)**: they are different on the mark scheme.
core.h: The five colours you must learn
core.p: You must learn the five colours as ion–colour pairs. Exam questions often give a flame colour and ask for the ion, or give the ion and ask for the colour. Memorise them with a mnemonic or by grouping: reds (crimson, orange-red), yellow, lilac, and green. Be careful with **lithium (crimson)** and **calcium (orange-red)**, which are both reddish; the mark scheme requires the right word for each.

bullets: Flame test identifies the **cation (metal ion)** only.
Anions (carbonate, halide, sulfate) need **separate chemical tests**.
A compound's name = metal from the flame test + non-metal from the anion test.
Sodium hydroxide precipitate tests also identify metal ions (and can separate Cu2+ and Ca2+ from others).
If two flame tests are similar, other tests or instrumental methods are used to check.
Always say **which ion** and the colour as evidence: 'the flame was lilac, so the compound contains potassium ions'.
Flame tests are **quick and simple** and need little apparatus.
The flame colour from the compound is independent of the anion, so potassium chloride and potassium nitrate both give lilac.
core.h: Using the flame colour to identify an unknown compound
core.p: In an exam you might be told that a white solid gives a lilac flame and is a chloride, and asked to name it. Here the flame test tells you the metal ion (potassium), and the other information tells you the anion, so the compound is potassium chloride. A flame test alone cannot identify the whole compound; it identifies the **metal ion**. To complete the identification you combine tests: flame test for the cation, tests for the anion (carbonate, halide, sulfate), and sometimes sodium hydroxide for metal hydroxide precipitates. This links to the other triple topics in 4.8.3.

bullets: A **mixture of ions** can give a flame colour that is a combination or dominated by one ion.
**Sodium's yellow** is intense and can **mask** the colours of other ions, especially lilac potassium.
**Contamination** (e.g. from an unclean wire or from sodium on hands) gives a false yellow.
Flame colours can be **subjective**: different people may describe the same colour differently.
Some colours are **similar** (crimson lithium and orange-red calcium) and hard to distinguish by eye.
Flame tests do not work for every metal ion and cannot give the **concentration** of an ion.
Small amounts of an ion may not give a visible colour (poor **sensitivity**).
These limitations are why **instrumental methods** are used in industry.
core.p: If a sample contains **more than one metal ion**, the strongest or brightest colour can **hide** the others, so a flame test may give a misleading result. The classic example is **sodium**, whose bright yellow colour masks lilac (potassium) and other colours. Because sodium compounds are so common (even in tap water, glass and fingerprints), traces of sodium can show yellow in the flame and confuse the result. This is one of the main reasons scientists prefer instrumental methods such as flame emission spectroscopy for mixtures.

bullets: **Flame test**: simple, cheap, quick, but subjective and unsuitable for mixtures or tiny amounts.
**Flame emission spectroscopy**: accurate, **rapid**, **sensitive** (detects tiny amounts) and works on **small samples**.
The emission spectrum of each ion is unique, so a mixture can be identified from the set of lines.
The machine can also give the **concentration** of the ions, as intensity relates to the amount.
Instrumental methods remove the problem of subjective colour judgement.
They are used in forensics, environmental monitoring and medicine.
Instrumental methods need expensive equipment and training.
The method still depends on electrons dropping energy levels and emitting light.
core.h: Flame tests compared with instrumental methods
core.p: Instrumental methods such as **flame emission spectroscopy** also use the light given out by excited ions, but the light is analysed by a machine that produces a **line spectrum**, rather than being judged by eye. This makes the analysis much more accurate and able to deal with mixtures. You will study instrumental methods in more detail in the separate topic, but for flame tests you should be able to compare the two approaches.

bullets: **Same type of flame**: a roaring (blue) Bunsen flame each time.
**Clean the wire** in acid and flame until no colour remains, between each test.
Use a **similar amount** of each sample.
Use **fresh** samples and a fresh wire or splint.
Observe in similar **lighting** (a darker room helps with faint colours such as lilac).
Record the colour **immediately** because it can fade quickly.
Repeat the test to check for **reproducibility**.
The independent variable is the **metal ion**; the dependent variable is the **flame colour**.
core.h: Controlling variables and making a flame test fair
core.p: A reliable flame test depends on **controlling the conditions**. If one test is done in a hot blue flame and another in a yellow flame, the colours cannot be compared. If the wire is not cleaned between samples, the colour from the previous sample contaminates the next. Variables to control include the type of flame, the cleanliness of the wire, the amount of sample and the heating time.

bullets: **Wear eye protection** (goggles) because acid and metal salts can splash and the flame can spit.
**Tie back long hair**, secure loose clothing, and keep flammables away from the flame.
**Hydrochloric acid** is an irritant (and corrosive at higher concentrations): use dilute acid, avoid contact.
The **wire loop becomes very hot**: allow it to cool before handling, and place it safely.
**Metal compounds** can be harmful or irritant: avoid touching them and wash hands after.
**Bunsen burners**: light correctly, use the blue flame, and turn to the safety (yellow) flame when not in use.
Work in a **well-ventilated** area, and dispose of waste as instructed.
Handle splints with tongs and put used splints in water.
core.p: Flame tests involve open flames, hot wires and corrosive or irritant chemicals. A good safety answer states the **hazard**, the **risk** and the **precaution**. Metal compounds can also be harmful; copper compounds are harmful if swallowed and irritant, and some salts are toxic.

bullets: Group 1 metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) show **similar chemistry** but **different flame colours**.
**Calcium** is a Group 2 metal; its compounds give an orange-red flame.
**Copper** is a transition metal; its compounds are often blue or green and give a green flame.
**Atomic structure**: electrons occupy energy levels; excitation and emission explain flame colours.
**Metal hydroxide precipitates** can confirm Cu2+ (blue precipitate) and Ca2+ (white precipitate).
**Anion tests** (carbonate, sulfate, halide) identify the rest of the compound.
**Instrumental methods** replace and improve flame tests in modern analysis.
**Fireworks** are a real-world use of the flame colours of metal compounds.
core.h: Linking flame tests to the rest of the course
core.p: Flame tests fit into the identification of ions in separate chemistry. Metals can also be identified using **sodium hydroxide solution** to give coloured precipitates (see 4.8.3), and anions by their own chemical tests. Flame tests also link to **atomic structure** (electrons in energy levels), the **periodic table** (alkali metals and their compounds), and the **uses of metals** (copper in electrical wires, calcium in bones and cement). In a Paper 2 question about identifying a salt you might need all of these ideas together.

bullets: A yellow flame is strong evidence for sodium but may hide other ions.
A weak lilac colour can be easily missed or masked: say 'a faint lilac flame suggests potassium'.
Ask whether the wire was **clean** (to rule out contamination).
**Repeating** the test improves reliability.
A **confirmatory test** (hydroxide precipitate or instrumental method) increases confidence.
The test works on **ions in compounds**; metal atoms in pure metals can also colour flames but this is less common at GCSE.
The method is **destructive** (the sample is burned/used up), but the quantity is small.
Flame tests are more reliable for **single-ion** samples than for mixtures.
core.h: Higher-level reasoning and evaluating the evidence
core.p: A good answer does not just recall colours; it evaluates how confident we can be in the result. If a flame test gives yellow, it could be sodium, or it could be a sodium impurity hiding another ion. A confident conclusion needs a clean wire, a repeat, and a confirmatory test (for example sodium hydroxide). Examiners reward answers that show an awareness that flame tests are **evidence for** an ion rather than proof.

bullets: **Describe** answers use sequence words (first, then, finally) and give the observation, e.g. 'the flame turned lilac'.
**Explain** answers use a reason connector (because, so, which) and mention excited electrons and light emitted.
**Evaluate** answers give one point for the test and one against, then a judgement such as 'useful for a quick check but not for mixtures'.
Always link the colour to the **ion** with its charge, e.g. 'lilac flame, so potassium ions K+ are present'.
If a table of results is given, match **each** sample to a colour and ion; do not skip rows.
State a **control**: clean the wire between samples so earlier samples do not contaminate the next flame.
Name the **hazard and precaution** together: dilute HCl is an irritant so wear eye protection; the wire loop is hot so let it cool.
Do not say the flame test shows the **amount** of ion; it is only qualitative.
core.h: Writing exam-quality answers: describe, explain and evaluate
core.p: Flame test questions use three command words and each needs a different kind of answer. **Describe** means say what you do and what you see, in order: clean the loop in dilute hydrochloric acid, dip it in the sample, hold it in the blue flame, record the colour. **Explain** means give the reason, which is that the heat excites electrons in the metal ion and they release the extra energy as light of a colour that depends on the metal. **Evaluate** means weigh strengths and limitations, so you comment on masking, contamination, subjectivity and the fact that only the metal ion is identified. Practise writing one answer to each command word, using the labelled set-up and the five ion-colour pairs from the diagrams.

exam: Typical question: 'Describe how to carry out a flame test' (usually **3-4 marks**): clean the wire in acid, dip in sample, place in blue flame, observe colour.
'Name the ion' questions give a colour and expect the **ion with its charge** (e.g. Ca2+) or at least the metal name; write both if unsure.
Learn the **five ion–colour pairs** exactly: Li+ crimson, Na+ yellow, K+ lilac, Ca2+ orange-red, Cu2+ green.
For a **limitation** question (1-2 marks) say that **sodium's yellow masks other colours** or that the test is **subjective**.
For 'compare flame tests with instrumental methods' write: instrumental methods are **faster, more accurate, more sensitive and use small samples**, and work with mixtures.
For a 6-mark question about identifying an unknown salt, plan: flame test (cation), then hydroxide precipitate to confirm, then anion tests; link each result to an ion.
Use the command word: **describe** = what you do and see; **explain** = the reason (electrons excited, light emitted).
For safety, state a hazard and precaution: acid is an irritant so wear eye protection; the wire is hot so allow it to cool.
In data questions, match the colours in a table to ions and state the conclusion with the evidence.
If told the sample is a **mixture**, mention masking.
A yellow flame alone does not prove sodium is the only metal present; say 'sodium is present'.

mistakes.r: It identifies the metal ion (cation) only; other tests are needed for the anion.
mistakes.w: Saying a flame test identifies the whole compound.

mistakes.r: Lithium gives a crimson flame; calcium gives an orange-red flame.
mistakes.w: Describing lithium as 'red' and calcium as 'red'.
Describing potassium as 'purple' or 'pink' without lilac.

mistakes.r: Clean the loop with hydrochloric acid and heat until there is no colour, to avoid contamination.
mistakes.w: Not cleaning the wire between samples.

mistakes.r: Use a hot, blue (non-luminous) flame so the colour is not hidden.
Some ions mask others (e.g. sodium's yellow), so it can be misleading for mixtures.
mistakes.w: Saying a flame test always works for mixtures.

mistakes.r: The colour comes from the metal ion.
mistakes.w: Saying the colour comes from the anion (e.g. chloride).

mistakes.r: Flame tests are qualitative; they do not tell you the amount.

summary: For triple science you must know that flame tests identify metal ions: lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red and copper(II) green. You must be able to describe the method, understand that mixtures can mask colours, and compare flame tests with instrumental methods.

terms.d: A test in which a sample is heated in a flame; the colour of the flame identifies the metal ion present.
A positively charged particle formed when a metal atom loses electrons, e.g. Na+, Ca2+.
A positively charged ion; the metal ion is the cation in a compound.
A deep red colour; the flame colour of lithium ions.
A pale purple colour; the flame colour of potassium ions.
The flame colour of calcium ions.
A wire made of a nickel–chromium alloy, used as a loop to hold the sample in the flame.
A hot, clean Bunsen flame with the air hole open; does not hide the colour from the sample.
Unwanted substances mixed with a sample, causing a false result.
When the colour of one ion hides the colour of another in a mixture.
A test that tells you what is present but not how much.
An analytical technique that uses a machine rather than human judgement.
An instrumental method in which the light from a heated sample is analysed to identify ions and measure their concentration.
An electron that has absorbed energy and moved to a higher energy level.
How small an amount of a substance can be detected by a method.
Two or more substances that are not chemically joined; in a mixture of ions some flame colours may be masked.

worked.q: A student heats a sample of a white solid in a Bunsen flame. The flame is lilac. Name the metal ion that is present. (1 mark)

worked.ans: Clean the nichrome loop in acid and flame; dip it in the compound; place it in a blue flame; the colour (e.g. green for copper) identifies the metal ion.
worked.q: Describe how to carry out a flame test to identify a metal ion in a compound. (4 marks)
steps: Clean the wire loop by dipping in dilute hydrochloric acid and heating in the flame until no colour is seen (1).
Dip the clean loop into the sample (1).
Hold the loop in the hot blue part of the Bunsen flame (1).
Observe and record the colour of the flame (1); match it to the ion.

worked.ans: The sample contains sodium, but it cannot be concluded that it contains only sodium because the yellow flame can mask other colours; further tests are needed.
worked.q: A sample gives a yellow flame. A student says it contains only sodium ions. Evaluate the student's conclusion. (3 marks)
steps: Yellow flame is evidence of sodium ions (1).
But sodium's strong yellow colour can mask other ions such as potassium (1).
Another test or flame emission spectroscopy is needed to confirm that no other ions are present (1).
